Let’s dive into Chapter 10: Measuring Success and Realizing the Benefits of Lean.
When it comes to Lean, how do you actually know if all your hard work is paying off? Well, it really comes down to measuring what matters most—focusing on both the clear, visible wins and those less obvious, but just as important, benefits that show up over time.
Now, measurement in Lean isn’t about drowning in spreadsheets or building fancy dashboards that nobody uses. It’s about choosing a handful of key indicators that truly tell the story. Are you delivering more value to your customers? Cutting out waste? Getting better, bit by bit, every day?
Here are a few of the classic Lean performance measures you’ll want to keep an eye on:
First, there’s lead time—the total time from when a customer asks for something to when you deliver it. Then, quality measures like defect rates, how often errors pop up, or the number of customer complaints. Productivity’s another big one: think output per person, or how much you’re getting out of your resources. And don’t forget employee engagement—how many people are taking part in improvements, sharing ideas, or feeling satisfied in their work?
Let’s make this real. Imagine a manufacturer tracking how long it takes to fill an order, counting defects per thousand units, and seeing what percentage of employees are jumping into daily problem-solving. Or picture a hospital looking at patient wait times, how often patients need to come back, and how involved staff are in improvement projects.
Here’s something to pay attention to—there’s a balance between quick wins and long-term health. Sure, you might see dramatic improvements early on. But keeping those gains takes regular check-ins, learning from what doesn’t work, and being willing to adjust as you go. That’s just part of the Lean journey.
And Lean isn’t just about the numbers. Some of the best benefits are harder to quantify—a team that feels energized and engaged, a workplace where trust and collaboration are the norm, and a reputation for being reliable and responsive. These intangibles might be tricky to measure, but honestly, they’re often the most valuable things you’ll gain.
Remember to celebrate progress—no matter how small. Every win helps reinforce the habits and mindsets that keep Lean alive. And when you share stories of what’s working—and what you’ve learned along the way—you help spread Lean thinking throughout your whole organization.
